description: Describes the operational frequency spectrum the device is designed to handle. It's trying to measure or validate the usable bandwidth of the chipset. This is validated under the general operating conditions of VDD1 (Amplifier drain bias voltage) = +5V, IDQ (Quiescent drain supply current) = 110mA, VSS2 (Switch negative bias voltage) = -3.3V, VDD2 (Switch positive supply voltage) = +3.3V, and TCASE (Case temperature) = 25°C.

Indicates the amplification factor of the amplifier when the input signal is small enough not to cause significant non-linearity. It's trying to measure or validate the amplifier's linear gain. This is typically validated under small input signal conditions at a specific frequency (e.g., in the mid-range of the overall frequency range) and under the general operating conditions (VDD1 = +5V, IDQ = 110mA, VSS2 = -3.3V, VDD2 = +3.3V, TCASE = 25°C).

Measures the variation in gain across the specified frequency range. It's trying to measure or validate how consistent the amplifier's gain is over its operational bandwidth. This is validated by sweeping the input frequency across the entire 0.01 MHz to 200 MHz range and measuring the gain at multiple points, ensuring it stays within the specified ±0.5 dB deviation under the general operating conditions.

Indicates how much of the input signal is reflected back from the amplifier's input port. A higher (more positive) S11 value (in dB) means less reflection and a better impedance match. It's trying to measure or validate the input impedance match of the amplifier. This is validated across the specified frequency range under the general operating conditions.

Indicates how much of the output signal is reflected back into the amplifier's output port from the load. A higher (more positive) S22 value (in dB) means less reflection and a better impedance match. It's trying to measure or validate the output impedance match of the amplifier. This is validated across the specified frequency range under the general operating conditions.

Represents the output power level at which the amplifier's gain has dropped by 1 dB compared to its ideal linear gain. It's a key metric for determining the maximum linear output power capability of the amplifier. It's trying to measure or validate the amplifier's output power capability before significant non-linearity. This is validated by increasing the input power to the amplifier until the output power deviates by 1 dB from the linear response. The specific note 'Measurement taken at POUT (Output Power) per tone = 5dBm' primarily applies to the OIP3/OIP2 measurements, but the core measurement is gain compression under the general operating conditions.

A theoretical point (extrapolated from measured data) where the power of the desired fundamental signals would be equal to the power of the third-order intermodulation distortion products. It's a critical metric for linearity, indicating how well the amplifier can handle multiple input signals without generating unwanted interference. It's trying to measure or validate the amplifier's intermodulation distortion performance. This is validated using a two-tone test where two input signals of equal amplitude are applied, resulting in an POUT (Output Power) of 5dBm per tone. The third-order intermodulation products are measured, and OIP3 is calculated under the general operating conditions.

Similar to OIP3, but for second-order intermodulation distortion products. It's another metric for linearity, particularly important in broadband systems where second-order products can fall in-band. It's trying to measure or validate the amplifier's second-order intermodulation distortion performance. This is validated using a two-tone test where two input signals of equal amplitude are applied, resulting in an POUT (Output Power) of 5dBm per tone. The second-order intermodulation products are measured, and OIP2 is calculated under the general operating conditions.

Measures the amount of noise added by the amplifier to the signal. A lower noise figure indicates a better signal-to-noise ratio at the output. It's trying to measure or validate the amplifier's noise performance. This is validated using a noise source and a noise figure meter under the general operating conditions.

Measures the signal attenuation (loss) when the device is operating in its bypass switch mode, meaning the signal passes through the internal switch without going through the amplifier. It's trying to measure or validate the signal loss incurred by the bypass path. This is validated under the general operating conditions (VDD1 = +5V, IDQ = 110mA, VSS2 = -3.3V, VDD2 = +3.3V, TCASE = 25°C) with the switch engaged in bypass mode.

Indicates the input return loss when the device is operating in its bypass switch mode. It's trying to measure or validate the input impedance match of the bypass path. This is validated across the specified frequency range with the switch in bypass mode, under the general operating conditions.

Indicates the output return loss when the device is operating in its bypass switch mode. It's trying to measure or validate the output impedance match of the bypass path. This is validated across the specified frequency range with the switch in bypass mode, under the general operating conditions.

Represents the input power level at which the amplifier's gain (in bypass switch mode) has dropped by 1 dB compared to its ideal linear gain. It's trying to measure or validate the maximum input power capability of the bypass path before significant non-linearity occurs. This is validated by increasing the PIN (Input Power) to the device (in bypass mode) until the output power deviates by 1 dB from the linear response under the general operating conditions.

Similar to IP1dB, but indicates the input power level at which the gain (in bypass switch mode) has dropped by 0.1 dB. This offers a more sensitive indicator of the onset of non-linearity. It's trying to measure or validate a more precise point of the bypass path's linear input power capability. This is validated by increasing the PIN (Input Power) to the device (in bypass mode) until the output power deviates by 0.1 dB from the linear response under the general operating conditions.

The theoretical input power level at which the power of the desired fundamental signals would be equal to the power of the third-order intermodulation distortion products, when the device is in bypass switch mode. It's trying to measure or validate the linearity performance of the bypass path against intermodulation distortion. This is validated using a two-tone test where two input signals are applied, each at an PIN (Input Power) of 14dBm. The third-order intermodulation products are measured, and IIP3 is calculated, all under the general operating conditions.
